title: DB-00 schema foundation and test harness

role_assignments._run_id_disambiguation: /claude/r0_steward (Anthropic) is THIS package's Integration Owner and must record its own capability declaration before this package leaves backlog. /root/r0_steward (OpenAI Codex) is a DIFFERENT run: it is the Integration Owner of WP-0A-A0-001 and WP-0A-CON-001 and is named in open_blockers solely because it must countersign the amendments made to those two packages and record the WP-0A-CON-001 npm run check addendum. Neither run substitutes for the other. Independent testing flagged the near-identical names as ambiguous; both are intended.

independence.cross_vendor_exception: prefer_cross_vendor_review is NOT satisfied: every assigned run is Anthropic claude-opus-5. The Decision Register (§ cross-vendor review) permits this only as an explicit exception - 'if there is no cross-vendor capacity, use an independent agent per run and record the exception'. Each of the five roles is a separate agent run with its own capability declaration and no run reviewed, tested, or integrated its own work. The Integration Owner must carry this exception forward; it is not waived and it is not equivalent to cross-vendor review.

required_human_authorities: Product Owner and A0 to decide the service path (supabase-js with the service-role key, or a direct driver with per-request SET LOCAL role), due before G1.
purpose: The first application code in this repository. RFC-2026-015 closed DATA-DEC-01 (`app`) and DATA-DEC-02 (a wrapper command contract, no tool named), which is exactly what the data package says gates the DB-00 merge and the start of DB-00 coding. This increment lands the batch 000 migration, the deterministic command contract, and the half of the schema lint decidable from the repository. The half needing a live Postgres is wired to REFUSE: this host has no psql, pg_ctl or docker and the repository forbids adding a dependency, so a harness that printed a pass would be the largest false clean run this repository has produced -- on the one surface where a false pass means tenant data.

include: Batch 000: the app and private schemas, the approved extension set, and the updated_at helper
The Makefile command contract with every target the data package names, and the wrapper behind it
The schema lint rules decidable from migration text, including the ENABLE-vs-FORCE rule the specified lint misses
Behaviour tests: each lint rule shown to reject before it is trusted, and every live target shown to refuse without a database
exclude: Any tenant table, and therefore any RLS policy. WP-0A-A0-007 carries a Proposed decision on the policy shape every later batch would inherit; migration invariant 1 forbids rewriting a merged migration, so writing the shape now would commit batches 010..180 to it.
Choosing a migration runner. DATA-DEC-02 fixes the contract, not the tool.
The live half of the harness: seed replay, RLS smoke and the acceptance tests. They need a provisioned test database.

amends_without_owning.rationale: The CI workflow is A0-only root configuration and A0 is the author here. One line inside the negative-control step is corrected -- the number it reports -- and no step is added, removed or reordered. The branch mapping is pinned whole in a test, and the integrity manifest records the digests of the protected files this branch edits.

acceptance_criteria: Batch 000 creates the app and private schemas with DATA-DEC-01's approved name, grants nothing to a client role, and touches no Supabase-managed schema.
Every target the data package names is reachable through make, sets LC_ALL=C and TZ=UTC, and prints a stable summary line whether it passes or fails.
Every target needing a database exits non-zero without one and names DB_TEST_URL. None reports a pass it cannot earn.
A connection string never reaches stdout or stderr.
Each schema lint rule is shown to REJECT a violating input, not merely to pass batch 000.
The lint rejects ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY without FORCE, which the lint rule the data package specifies would pass.
npm run check stays green with no test skipped and no declared floor lowered.
required_tests: Each lint rule rejects a violating input
Every live target refuses without a database
db-verify fails as a whole and names what is missing
rollback_or_forward_fix: Revert through a reviewed revert PR. The migration has never been applied to any database -- no instance is provisioned -- so there is no deployed schema to roll back, and the command contract and lint are inert without one.
open_blockers: The live half runs in CI and nowhere else. A Postgres service container gives db-migrate-clean, db-schema-lint and db-rls-smoke a real database on every pull request; all NINE migration batches apply -- 000, 001, 002, 003, 004, 010, 011, 020 and 021, counted from the tree rather than carried forward -- and the schema lint passes. The count read "five" from the moment batch 004 was added two commits later in the same night, on the same package, in a commit whose own blocker text says "Batch 004 exists"; C0's review D10 found it. This DEVELOPMENT HOST still has no psql, pg_ctl or docker, so the targets refuse locally and every live change is proven by a CI round, not from a shell. db-migrate-upgrade and db-seed-replay remain unproven for a different reason: neither has a fixture to run against, and both say so rather than reporting a pass.

The negative control's reported count now counts FAILED CASE LINES rather than every indented line containing a parenthesis, which had been sweeping the coverage report and the authz-proof lines in with them. A2 Industry found it by reading the CI output rather than the step, and reported it instead of fixing it because the step is A0's.

The control itself was never wrong: it greps case ids, and it bit correctly on every family. Only the sentence describing what it had done was wrong -- which is the kind of defect that survives longest, because nothing it guards ever fails.

The CI negative control runs PER TABLE FAMILY as of 2026-09-06, and each entry requires a failed case whose id matches that table's own pattern. The single-table version reported '10 of 28' and then '10 of 76' -- the same ten, because every one names app.workspaces -- so batch 020's 41 cases were never exercised by it and the number kept being reported as though it meant something. A control that grows stale as the suite grows is worse than none.

BATCH 030 ADDS THE FIFTH, SIXTH AND SEVENTH ENTRIES -- one for each table it creates -- and one of them is a shape this control has not had before. app.industry_assignments is an ordinary tenant entry: disabling row level security there lets tenant A read tenant B's assignment, lets a member scoped to one Business read another's, and lets the suspended member and the service identity read rows they must not see; four cases match its pattern.

app.industry_packs AND app.industry_pack_versions ARE THE NEW SHAPE, and the reason is recorded in the workflow beside the entries rather than only here. They belong to NO WORKSPACE, so there is no tenant boundary for the control to dissolve, and batch 030 grants no client role any privilege on them at all (RFC-2026-012 §2/3: the read allowlist starts empty and grows only by RFC). Every client case against them is a PRIVILEGE-layer refusal, and disabling row level security does not restore a grant nobody made -- so none of those cases would notice. The entries bite through the ONE grant that exists: app_worker holds SELECT and no policy, which is batch 010's shape for making a service denial attributable to RLS rather than to a forgotten GRANT, so with RLS off the service reads the catalog and `service-sees-zero-*` fails. EACH OF THOSE TWO ENTRIES THEREFORE RESTS ON EXACTLY ONE CASE. That is a weaker control than the others and it is named as one: tests/db/identity/identity-isolation.test.mjs asserts each of those cases by id, by outcome kind and by identity helper, so deleting the case fails the build instead of leaving an entry that disables something nothing notices. It stops being weak the day an RFC opens the read allowlist, which is the same day more cases on those tables become RLS-decided.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN: the GENERAL rule. Nothing yet fails the build when a future batch adds a table and no entry, because deciding what a "table family" is -- app.workspace_settings and app.workspace_invitations have no entry of their own and are covered by app.workspaces' -- is a judgement A0 owns and is not derivable from a migration's text. A per-batch pin is what a batch can be held to; the general rule needs the definition first. Batch 030 makes that definition harder rather than easier, and says so: a rule phrased as "every table needs an entry" would now have to answer what a global table's entry is FOR.

A NUMBER THIS STEP PRINTS IS NOT WHAT IT SAYS IT IS, found by reading batch 030's own CI round (run 34035745383, head aea9582) rather than by argument. Each entry echoes "$(grep -c "^  .*(" control.log) case(s) noticed", and that pattern matches every output line starting with two spaces and containing a parenthesis -- which includes the §12.6 coverage report `make db-rls-smoke` prints for every assertion it cannot carry, and the `db-authz-proofs` lines after it. The run reported 18 for app.workspaces, 21 for app.business_profiles, 18 for app.page_context_profiles, 32 for app.workspace_member_scopes, 21 for app.industry_assignments and 9 for each of the two global tables. Those are UPPER BOUNDS on failed cases, not counts: the single-table version of this control historically reported '10 of 28' for app.workspaces, and 18 here is consistent with the same ten plus a constant non-case offset. The exact split cannot be read from a green run, because control.log is only printed when the control FAILS.

It is recorded rather than fixed. The control itself is sound -- what it requires is that a case MATCHING THE TABLE'S PATTERN failed, which is a grep over ids and not this number -- so the defect is in the reporting line, and the step belongs to A0. Batch 030 added three entries and changed no step logic, which is what its amendment declaration says. But the number is the same class of thing 021's paragraph above objects to, and a control that overstates itself in the direction of looking thorough is worth naming before somebody quotes it.

RFC-2026-020 is APPROVED (2026-09-06) and batch 011 lands it: db/foundation/migrations/011_authorization_helpers.sql creates app_authz, its single narrow SELECT policy on app.workspace_members, three SECURITY DEFINER helpers it owns, and the roster policy implementing §8.1's "Member list SELECT: Owner Y, Admin Y". The approval's condition -- §6.2 discharged by EXECUTION, never by citation -- is met: see the entry below and evidence/WP-0A-DB-00/a1-batch-011-execution-2026-09-06.md.

STILL OPEN, and NOT closed by this batch: RFC-2026-017 §3's table gains a fourth row for app_authz, and A0 owns that edit. RFC-2026-020 §7 proposes the amendment and does not make it; batch 011 does not make it either, because an approved decision is not the implementing batch's to amend. THAT PREDICTION ABOUT BATCH 021 WAS WRONG, AND 021 SAYS SO RATHER THAN QUIETLY DOING SOMETHING ELSE. This blocker read "batch 021's workspace_member_scopes will need app_authz to have a policy on it too, by the same reasoning and with the same width test; that is 021's to propose". It cannot: RFC-2026-020 §5/3 gives app_authz EXACTLY ONE policy, §6.1/6 pins its grants to USAGE on schema app plus four columns of app.workspace_members, `authzLint` asserts both, and 011's own apply-time block raises when the policy count is not one -- so a second policy would make an APPLIED migration's self-assertion false on any database the set is re-applied to. An approved decision is not the implementing batch's to amend, which is the sentence 011 and 020 both wrote when they refused a cell.

SO 021 TOOK THE NARROWER ROUTE: its five scope helpers are SECURITY INVOKER and read app.workspace_member_scopes AS THE CALLER, and the width is one policy 021 writes and pins -- `user_id = (select auth.uid()) and app.is_active_member(workspace_id)`. No new role, no new grant to app_authz, no second exemption. 021's own apply-time block re-asserts app_authz's policy count and its absence of privilege on the new table AFTER 021 has run, which is the half 011's block cannot reach because it runs before this file exists. The coupling 020's header warns about does not apply: 020 rejects joining app.workspace_members from a policy because that table's policy set belongs to two other batches and can move, whereas 021 creates its table, writes both of its policies and pins the one the helpers read.

A0 DEFECT (the exemption register could not carry the form RFC-2026-016 §4 sanctions) -- CLOSED by batch 011. WAS: the corroboration rule in scripts/db/run.mjs rejected a role-scoped row unless the role held rolbypassrls or rolsuper, so the only exemption the register could corroborate was the role ATTRIBUTE, which is the form §4 was REPLACING. app_authz's policy could not be registered at all; a row for it would have failed the lint.

IS NOW: roleScopedCorroboration accepts either a role attribute OR a policy in schema app naming the role, and the widening is falsifiable in both directions. A row claiming a policy the catalog does not show is still refused. For the policy form the row's `table` is corroborable -- unlike an attribute, which is database-wide -- so a row claiming app.X while the catalog shows the policy on app.Y is refused. And roleScopedCompleteness reads it the other way: a policy naming a role OUTSIDE the request path with no register row is refused. Request-path roles are excluded because a policy naming anon, authenticated or service_role is §8.1 being implemented, not an exemption, and demanding a row for each would fill the register with the access matrix and make it unreadable.

NO ROW IS ADDED for app_authz, and that is the rule working rather than an omission. The snapshot describes the provisioned instance, which does not have batch 011, so the policy is not in the catalog and a row for it would be refused -- correctly. The completeness pass is what will force that row in the day 011 reaches the instance and the snapshot records its policy. Six cases in test-kits/db/foundation-contract.test.mjs construct both directions, and the accept direction is exercised with a synthesised app_authz policy rather than only with the maximal exemption.

RFC-2026-020 §6.2 -- DISCHARGED BY EXECUTION, both claims, CI run 34017080120 on head 68d1432. scripts/db/authz-proofs.mjs runs behind `make db-rls-smoke` against the same postgres:17 service container, so a failure fails the build with no workflow change. `db-authz-proofs: ok -- 6 claim(s) discharged by execution`.

§6.2/8: the naive recursive member-list policy raises `SQLSTATE 42P17: infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "workspace_members"`, recorded verbatim. §6.2/9: the SECURITY DEFINER helper is NOT inlined -- EXPLAIN (VERBOSE) shows `Output: app.workspace_member_role('...'::uuid)` with no scan of app.workspace_members.

THE CONTROL IS THE PART TO REVIEW. The obvious control -- copy the helper, flip to SECURITY INVOKER, show that one inlines -- passes while proving NOTHING, for two independent reasons either of which alone is fatal: PostgreSQL will not inline a SQL function carrying a SET clause (the helper has `set search_path = ''`), and will not inline one with a FROM clause in any security mode (the helper reads a table). Both sides would have read "not inlined" and the discriminator would never have discriminated. The pair therefore differs in prosecdef and nothing else -- same body, no SET clause, no FROM -- using the shape RFC-2026-020 §2.4 already measured being inlined on the instance. Measured: the INVOKER half's plan contains its body (`Output: (((NULLIF(current_setting(...))::jsonb ->> 'sub'::text))::uuid`), the DEFINER half's contains a call. If the definer half ever inlines, the proof reports the decision WRONG and the batch must be reverted rather than worked around; that branch is executed locally against a fake runner.

BATCH 011's OWN OPEN ITEMS, recorded by A1 rather than left for a reviewer to find.

THE HELPERS' SCHEMA is `app`, and this DISAGREES with a document this manifest declares as its own input. docs/sprint-0a/sprint-0a-core-erd-rls-retention-th.md:71 gives `private` the row "authorization helpers, secret references, raw webhook, worker payload, reconciliation | ไม่มี direct grant | Server/worker ผ่าน typed service เท่านั้น". Two thirds of that row cannot hold at once for THIS helper: a policy written TO authenticated that calls a function is evaluated as the CALLER, so authenticated must hold EXECUTE on it and USAGE on its schema -- and putting the helpers in `private` therefore requires granting authenticated USAGE on `private`, which is the "no direct grant" column of the same row, and which would put private.as_user, private.as_suspended_user and private.set_updated_at inside the reach of every end user. That is a WIDER exposure than the one it avoids. The row is not wrong; its model is a helper called by a server or worker through a typed service, a command path where `private` is exactly right, and it did not anticipate a helper called by the policy machinery on the request path. RFC-2026-020 is Approved, newer, sits at position 1 of the conflict order where the data package sits at 4, contemplates the helper being EXECUTE-granted to authenticated in §6.3/12-13, and leaves the API and its schema to this batch in §8.

A THIRD SCHEMA IS NOT CREATED, and is carried open. `authz` would be narrower than `app` without touching `private`, but batch 000 created app and private under DATA-DEC-01, the schema lint pins our_schemas, and adding a third is a data-foundation decision belonging in an RFC rather than in the batch that happens to want it.

WHETHER PostgREST EXPOSES THESE AS RPC CANNOT BE CHECKED HERE. Measured read-only 2026-09-06: no role on the provisioned instance carries a pgrst.db_schemas setting in pg_db_role_setting. The exposed-schema list is platform configuration outside the database, so the catalog holds no evidence either way and no lint in this repository can check it -- a decision resting on it would be exactly the unfalsifiable shape RFC-2026-016 §4 retired "force where compatible" for being. So the helpers are built to be SAFE WHEN EXPOSED rather than safe because hidden: workspace_member_role and is_active_member answer only about the CALLER, asserted by a proof and an isolation case rather than assumed, and jwt_subject is granted to NOBODY -- it is called only from inside helpers that run as its owner and no policy names it, so a grant would be a callable surface, and an RPC endpoint wherever app is the exposed schema, with no caller.

§8.1's "Workspace UPDATE: Admin P" IS REFUSED, NOT FORGOTTEN. P is "passes per policy/explicit capability" and no document defines the capability set; RFC-2026-020 §8 says so and says the scope table that would carry it is batch 021's. Writing role in ('owner','admin') into the workspace UPDATE policy would not resolve a capability -- it would DELETE the distinction between Y and P and ship admin an unconditional grant nobody reviewed, which is the precise thing 010 said it was avoiding. "Member list SELECT" Owner Y and Admin Y ARE implemented; Editor's P is not, for the same reason.

THE CATALOG SNAPSHOT now describes a database the migration set has moved ahead of, and says so. Batch 011 is deliberately not applied to the provisioned instance -- one of its proofs constructs a knowingly-recursive policy in order to observe 42P17, and applying an unmerged authorization boundary to a live database so a lint passes is the inversion the lint exists to prevent. NO FIELD IS INVENTED for objects that are not there: there is no authz block, the gap is declared by name in not_applied_to_this_instance with a stated reason, taken_against_migrations is the digest of the APPLIED set, and the declaration must name files that exist and must name a TAIL of the ordered set, because a database missing a middle batch while holding later ones is DIVERGENT rather than behind. The absence is checked in BOTH directions: an authz block while the declaration stands is refused, and the block becomes REQUIRED the moment the declaration is withdrawn. RFC-2026-020 §6.1/1-6 are asked instead of the CI container, where the objects exist, through the same authzLint the snapshot path would call rather than a second copy that could drift. Two fields that ARE measurable on the instance were measured read-only and added rather than assumed: platform_auth_uid (verbatim pg_get_functiondef, which is what turns §5/4's inlined copy into a build failure if Supabase moves the original) and role_scoped_policies (all ten name authenticated).

BATCH 020's OWN OPEN ITEMS, recorded by A1 Business rather than left for a reviewer to find. Batch 020 lands app.business_profiles, app.business_profile_versions, app.page_context_profiles and app.page_context_profile_versions with their policies, grants and composite scope keys. Three things it deliberately does NOT do.

WORKSPACE LIFECYCLE VISIBILITY IS NOT ENFORCED ON THESE TABLES, and this is the one gap that is a gap rather than a refusal. §8.5 lists "lifecycle visibility" as part of a SELECT predicate, and batch 010's own workspace policy stops at `access_blocked` because §11.4 defines that transition as revoking sessions, connectors and jobs. A member of a workspace in `access_blocked` can still read its business and page rows. Closing it needs one of two things, neither of which is this batch's to take: a join to app.workspaces from these policies, which would make the width of business visibility a property of another module's policy set -- exactly the coupling RFC-2026-020 §5/5 removed for membership -- or a lifecycle-aware authorization helper, which must be owned by app_authz, whose grants RFC-2026-020 §6.1/6 pins to USAGE on schema app and a column-scoped SELECT on four columns of app.workspace_members, and which authzLint rejects any widening of. It is owed to an RFC plus batch 170 (grants/RLS/exposed surface hardening).

§8.1's EDITOR `P` ON "Business/Page INSERT/UPDATE/archive" IS NOT IMPLEMENTED, and that is a refusal on RFC-2026-020 §8's reasoning rather than an omission. `P` is "passes per policy/explicit capability" and no document in this repository defines the capability set; §7 names the machinery and puts the table that carries it, workspace_member_scopes, in batch 021. Writing `role in ('owner','admin','editor')` would delete the distinction between `Y` and `P` and ship the editor an unconditional grant nobody reviewed. The isolation case `editor-a-cannot-create-a-business` asserts the default-deny so it cannot be mistaken for a decided N.

§5's INVENTORY ROW FOR THIS MODULE READS "page_context_profiles, versions, bindings" AND NO BINDING TABLE IS CREATED. A channel binding carries social_account_id (§3.3), whose table is batch 110, and §6's registry gives the business-channel/social foreign key to batch 111; migration invariant 6 puts a cross-module FK in an integration batch and nowhere else. The registry's own description of 020 -- "business/page + immutable versions" -- omits bindings for that reason. Owed by 110/111.

WHAT BATCH 021 MUST CHANGE IN THIS SUITE, so it is not left to be rediscovered: §12.6 assertion 2 is recorded `partial` in SMOKE_COVERAGE, and the case `editor-a-sees-business-a2-until-batch-021` asserts that the editor CAN see the second business in their own workspace today. That is §8.1 being implemented -- Business/Page SELECT is Y for every active member and no scope row exists yet -- and it is asserted positively so that 021 narrowing it is a change to a test in a diff rather than a claim that quietly became false. §8.6 cases 3 and 4 are owed by 021 for the same reason.

TWO THINGS THIS INCREMENT CHANGED IN INHERITED FILES, recorded because neither is about batch 020's own tables and a reviewer would otherwise have to work out why they are in the diff. FIRST, scripts/db/run.mjs now holds the snapshot's `tenant_tables` to a COMPLETENESS rule in both directions -- every table created by a migration the instance has received must have a row, and a row for a table no such migration creates is a finding -- and the per-table rules, RFC-2026-017 §3's owner rule among them, moved into one exported `tenantTableLint` with it. That rule could not exist before 020: while the instance had every migration, a table missing from the list and a table that does not exist were indistinguishable, and every rule this repository writes about tenant tables is worth exactly what the guarantee that the list is complete is worth. It is what forces 020's four tables into the snapshot the day the instance receives the batch, rather than leaving that to whoever remembers. Four cases in test-kits/db/foundation-contract.test.mjs construct both directions. SECOND, the fixture catalog gained ONE symbol and not seven. `business_a3_archived` is there because §11.3 is a real clause in 020's page INSERT policy and asserting it needs an archived Business; the version rows are addressed by (parent, version_number), which 020 makes unique, so no version needs an id of its own and the cross-tenant cases still hold the target tenant's REAL business and page ids. The closed-set assertion in foundation-contract.test.mjs is now over §12.6's symbols PLUS a list a batch has to edit by name, so the catalog can grow only through a reviewed diff -- §12.6's list was written before any table existed and reading it as the complete universe of fixture rows would mean no batch could ever assert a rule about a state it happened not to enumerate.

RFC-2026-019 §5 is IMPLEMENTED here, and two of its three rules assert states measured true today rather than states someone must remember: authenticator is a member of anon, authenticated and service_role and of no service role, and no table in app is owned by app_command. The third records the owner of every SECURITY DEFINER function so the first one owned by app_command arrives in a diff.

What is NOT closed by this: RFC-2026-017 §3's present tense. No command function and no background worker exists, and a lint cannot create one. The rules hold the decision; the components are still missing, and that is what the tense is wrong about.

open_blockers[1] asked for the co-owner's signature on the role topology. A1 wrote its own record at evidence/WP-0A-DB-00/a1-countersignature-role-topology.md. READ THE VERDICT THERE: this manifest is written by A0 and does not speak for another role, so it does not restate it here.

What A0 can state, because it is a property of that document rather than a judgement about it: A1 re-measured the provisioned instance itself through ten read-only catalog queries rather than accepting A0's record, three of its findings contradict a record A0 wrote, and it declares in its own §0 that it is a subagent run in A0's vendor and model family assessing files it authored. It therefore does not satisfy independence.prefer_cross_vendor_review and does not lift the cross_vendor_exception this package already carries -- a second reading, not a second opinion.

The reservations that record raises are carried as the five blockers below, and they are open.

RESERVATION 1 (A1 §5.1) — REPAIRED, and the repair was then narrowed by C0's review D2. db/foundation/lint/rls-exemption-register.json exists and the schema lint reads it in BOTH directions, which is RFC-2026-016 §4's own wording and the difference between a control and a list: a table that is not forced with no row is refused, and a row whose exemption the catalog does not show is refused too -- because a register carrying exemptions nobody took cannot be read as complete, and completeness is the whole of what it proves about the tables that are NOT in it. Rows are held to the six fields the RFC names, to a known operation, and to a review date not older than the snapshot: an exemption does not age into permanence.

The register is EMPTY, and empty means something only because a non-empty one is checked. Six cases construct the situations rather than asserting on the file.

RESERVATION 2 (A1 §5.2) — REPAIRED, and the repair is what is now asserted. scripts/db/run.mjs asserts no service role is SUPERUSER as well as no service role holds BYPASSRLS, refuses a snapshot whose service_roles carry no superuser field at all (an unmeasured property must not read as a passing one), and pins the instance's superuser set the way it already pinned the bypass set. Measured 2026-09-06 on xtvtflkntpqfvflvdbwk: all three service roles rolsuper false; supabase_admin is the only rolsuper on the instance.

RESERVATION 3 (A1 §5.3/§5.4) — REPAIRED, and the correction is now a check rather than a comment. Batch 004 exists: it records both of batch 000's wrong claims (pgcrypto is not required for gen_random_uuid, which has been in pg_catalog since PG13; and `with schema public` was a no-op on the instance, where pgcrypto already lived in `extensions`), and it FAILS if gen_random_uuid is not resolvable unqualified or if pgcrypto is installed in public. That second assertion is what stops the CI/platform divergence returning: remove the shim line and this batch fails with the reason. Applied to the instance 2026-09-06 and the catalog snapshot retaken against migration set 7215963802260771.

000_foundation.sql's own text is unchanged: migration invariant 1 forbids rewriting an applied batch, which is why 003 corrected 002 the same way. The RFC status line inside its comment is still stale and is a decision-record status question, not a migration's.

What this repair COST, which was recorded nowhere until C0's review D3 measured it: because 000 and 004 are both applied and neither may be rewritten, the migration set became applicable only to a database where pgcrypto already exists outside `public`, and the only thing arranging that outside the platform was one line in a GitHub workflow. See the D3 entry below: the prerequisite is now part of `make db-migrate-clean` itself.

RESERVATION 4 (A1 §5.5) — REPAIRED at the call sites AND at the cause. The fixture and the invitation case now take the digest with pg_catalog's sha256(convert_to(...)), which resolves with no extension and no schema qualification; measured 2026-09-06 that it produces byte-identical output to extensions.digest(...,'sha256'), so no fixture identity moved. The cause was that the CI shim was MORE PERMISSIVE than the platform: batch 000's `create extension ... with schema public` is a no-op on the instance and succeeded in the container, so public.digest existed only in CI. The shim now installs pgcrypto in `extensions` where the platform has it, and the test that used to pin `public.digest(` now refuses any schema-qualified pgcrypto call.

Two consequences of that shim change were found later by C0. The pgcrypto placement has since moved out of the shim into db/foundation/prerequisites.sql, which db-migrate-clean applies itself (D3). And the reason attached to the test became false in both halves the moment the shim changed, because extensions.digest exists in the container now (D12). Both entries are below.

RESERVATION 5 (A1 §5.6) — REPAIRED, and the repair was then completed by C0's review D6. expectDeniedBy holds a case to the layer it declares, and the runner applies it to every case carrying deniedBy. A policy refusal always names the policy; anything else saying permission denied is the privilege layer; anything that classifies as neither fails rather than guessing. Silence stays silence: a case declaring no layer is not checked.

What that missed: a layer is not an attribution on its own. `permission denied for schema private` is 42501 and classifies as the same 'grant' layer as a refusal on the table under test, so the assertion said WHICH LAYER refused and never WHICH OBJECT. See the D6 entry below; a case now declares deniedOn beside deniedBy and the refusal must name that relation.

Tenant isolation is proven against the CI container and measured once against a provisioned Supabase instance, and the two prove different things. In CI, 115 isolation cases pass on every run -- 35 from batches 010/011, 40 added by batch 020 (41 minus the one batch 021 replaced) and 40 added by batch 021 -- and the NEGATIVE CONTROL now runs per table family: app.workspaces (010), app.business_profiles and app.page_context_profiles (020) and app.workspace_member_scopes (021), each disabled on its own with row level security re-enabled after it, and each requiring a failed case whose id matches that table's own pattern. What CI cannot establish is the platform: its roles come from db/foundation/ci/supabase-shim.sql and were created by us, so a green run means the policies still do what they did, never that this holds on Supabase. The BYPASSRLS measurement behind DATA-DEC-03 came from the provisioned instance and has no CI equivalent. §12.6 assertion 2 is now covered; 3 is still owed by batches 040 and 080, and 8's positive half still cannot be asserted without inventing a service permission §8.1 does not grant.

C0 CONTRACT REVIEW, 2026-09-06. The independent Reviewer run /claude/c0_contract_reviewer read the night's merged work and confirmed twelve defects. Its report is landed byte-for-byte at evidence/WP-0A-DB-00/c0-review-2026-09-06-night.md and is another run's record: it is not edited here, and the entries below dispose of it rather than restating it.

READ ITS §0 FIRST. C0 declares in its own words that it is a subagent spawned by A0 -- the author of everything it reviewed -- running in the same vendor and model family, on threads A0 chose. It therefore does NOT satisfy independence.prefer_cross_vendor_review, does not lift the cross_vendor_exception this package already carries, and must not be counted as the independent review this package owes. What it is: a second reading whose measurements against the tree stand on their own, every one of them re-runnable from the command or file:line it cites.

Disposition of the twelve: eight repaired here (D2, D3, D6, D7, D8, D9, D10, D12), one recorded without editing its source (D11), one carried open (D4), two belonging to other packages (D1 to WP-0A-CON-002, D5 to WP-0A-CON-008) and left alone. Each is an entry below.

D2 (MEDIUM-HIGH) — REPAIRED. WAS: the exemption register declared a granularity of role x table x operation and the lint enforced none of it. Rows were matched to a table by NAME alone, so a row scoped as narrowly as the shape allows -- {role: 'app_worker', operation: 'select'} -- bought its table a blanket pass, and the same row suppressed rls_enabled as well as rls_forced, which let one register row excuse a tenant table having no row level security at all.

IS NOW: the lint enforces what the catalog can CORROBORATE, and scripts/db/run.mjs and the register's own _what_the_catalog_can_corroborate say plainly what that is. relforcerowsecurity is a TABLE property -- one value for every role and every operation at once -- so it corroborates exactly one row, role '*' with operation 'all', and only such a row suppresses the unforced-table finding. rolbypassrls and rolsuper are ROLE properties holding for every table at once, so a row naming a role is checked against that role's own attributes and suppresses no table finding; naming a table in it narrows nothing. NOTHING in the snapshot is per-operation -- it counts a table's policies and never records which command one is for -- so an operation other than 'all' is refused as uncorroborable in either direction, which is the same unfalsifiable shape §4 retired 'force where compatible' for being. rls_enabled is not exemptible at all: RFC-2026-012 commits the whole client/database boundary to row level security and §4 retired only the FORCE condition.

Three new cases in test-kits/db/foundation-contract.test.mjs, and the ACCEPTED row in one of them is {role: 'service_role', operation: 'all'} -- corroborated by the catalog's measured roles_bypassing_rls -- so the accept direction is no longer always the maximal exemption.

D3 (MEDIUM) — REPAIRED. WAS: `make db-migrate-clean` was no longer self-sufficient. Batch 004 raises if pgcrypto is in `public` and batch 000 puts it there on any database nobody prepared; both are applied and migration invariant 1 forbids rewriting either, so the set was applicable only where pgcrypto already existed outside `public`. That held on the provisioned instance by the platform's doing and in CI by ONE LINE INSIDE A GITHUB WORKFLOW -- `psql -f db/foundation/ci/supabase-shim.sql` before the make target. The repository's own declared command could not apply its own migration set to a bare Postgres, and nothing recorded the cost.

IS NOW: the prerequisite is part of the declared command. db/foundation/prerequisites.sql holds the two statements the migration set actually requires -- `create schema if not exists extensions` and `create extension if not exists pgcrypto with schema extensions` -- and scripts/db/run.mjs applies it as the first step of migrate-clean, exposed as migrateCleanSteps() so a test asserts on the steps the target runs rather than on this file's text. It is deliberately NOT a migration: it sits outside db/foundation/migrations/, carries no batch number, joins no digest and reserves nothing, so the catalog snapshot's taken_against_migrations does not go stale (asserted).

The shim LOST those two lines and keeps everything that is genuinely Supabase emulation -- the auth schema, auth.uid(), the three platform roles -- and keeps its header saying what it is not. That is the part that makes the repair observable: CI no longer satisfies the prerequisite in advance, so the container reaching batch 000 with pgcrypto in `extensions` is now the command's doing, and if migrate-clean stops applying it, batch 004 fails the build. A test pins that the shim does not create pgcrypto.

EXECUTED, and this is the evidence rather than the argument. CI run 33995058177 on this branch, Database foundation step: `applied db/foundation/prerequisites.sql` followed by all six batches and `db-migrate-clean: ok in 309ms`, then `db-schema-lint: ok`. The shim no longer places pgcrypto, so that container reached batch 000 with pgcrypto in `extensions` because the COMMAND put it there. Batch 004 -- which raises on pgcrypto in `public` -- passed on a database nothing else had prepared for it. This host has no psql and no docker, so nothing here was executed locally.

WHAT THE CLAIM DOES NOT COVER, stated because the difference is exactly the kind that gets lost: `db-migrate-clean` is now self-sufficient in everything the REPOSITORY introduced. It is not self-sufficient in the PLATFORM's own surface. Batch 010 writes policies over auth.uid() and grants to anon, authenticated and service_role, and a Postgres with none of those is a Postgres the migration set cannot apply to at all. Supabase provides them; db/foundation/ci/supabase-shim.sql emulates them for CI and says in its own header that it is not Supabase. Moving THOSE into the command would mean a `create or replace function auth.uid()` running against a managed instance, which is a worse defect than the one this repaired.

D6 (MEDIUM-LOW) — REPAIRED. WAS: expectDeniedBy attributed a LAYER without attributing an OBJECT. `permission denied` is a catch-all, so `permission denied for schema private` -- the exact failure this harness produced on all seven no-effect cases -- classified as the same 'grant' layer as `permission denied for table workspace_invitations`. A case declaring deniedBy: 'grant' therefore passed when the refusal came from a privilege problem in the SCAFFOLDING rather than on the object under test.

IS NOW: db/foundation/test-helpers/rls-assertions.mjs carries denialObject() beside denialLayer(), reading which relation, schema or function the message names, and expectDeniedBy takes the case's declared { kind, name }. A refusal on a different object -- a schema where a table was claimed, a function, another table, or nothing named at all -- fails the case rather than satisfying it. run-isolation.mjs passes the declaration, and identity-isolation.test.mjs pins statically that deniedBy and deniedOn are declared together, that the declared object is one the case's own statement reaches, and that `private` -- the harness's own schema -- is never claimed as a subject.

The KIND is declared rather than inferred, and writing the four declarations is where this stopped being bookkeeping. Two of the cases are `authenticated`, which holds USAGE on schema app (010:390), so a read it may not make is refused on the TABLE: { table, workspace_invitations } for both. The other two are ANONYMOUS, and batch 010 grants anon nothing anywhere (010:386) while PUBLIC holds no USAGE on app either -- measured, catalog-snapshot public_grants.usage_on_app is false -- so an anonymous read never reaches a table at all: name resolution refuses it on the SCHEMA, { schema, app }. The first draft of this repair declared { table, workspaces } and { table, workspace_members } for those two, which would have turned CI red for the right reason. Recording it because the correction came from reading the grants and the snapshot rather than from the run, and because it is the finding's own lesson arriving one level in: an attribution nobody checked against the privilege topology is a guess.

Silence is still not a claim: a case declaring neither is checked for neither.

C0's other observation on this finding stands unrepaired and is not a defect: no live case declares deniedBy: 'policy', so in the live suite the discriminator only ever runs its catch-all arm. D7 (LOW, privilege path) — REPAIRED. WAS: `reset role;` was injected into a case's prelude by matching /\bprivate\.as_/ against the SQL AFTER parameter values had been inlined into it. A case whose parameter carried that literal text -- and the cases do pass free-text names like 'renamed by the service' -- would have had its own statement run as the administrative connection role instead of the identity under test. No fixture value triggered it and the escalation was confined to a rolled-back transaction; the shape was the defect.

IS NOW: the decision is taken from the STATEMENT before substitution, in scripts/db/rls-smoke.mjs, and the escaping of values is unchanged. bufferedDriver takes its query function as a seam so the SQL it assembles is observable, and a test drives it with a parameter containing `private.as_service`, asserts no reset is emitted, asserts the value still reaches the statement, and asserts a real identity call still gets its reset.

D8 (LOW, latent) — REPAIRED. WAS: the result boundary could be moved by data, and moved forward silently. One marker was selected before the statement and everything after its LAST occurrence was parsed, so a marker appearing in the statement's own output won the search: the region became a suffix of the real result whose first line was then eaten as a header, and a single occurrence in the final row yielded ZERO ROWS -- a PASS for expectNoRows and for half one of expectNoEffect. Separately, the EPILOGUE was inside the parsed region, so anything it printed became extra rows of the statement's result; that was safe only because the sole caller passes `rollback;`, and nothing in the signature or a test said an epilogue had to be silent.

IS NOW: the result is FENCED between two markers, and scripts/db/psql-driver.mjs counts them instead of searching. Each marker select prints its marker exactly twice -- column name, then value -- so 2 and 2 is the only shape the driver emits; any other count means output somewhere carried a marker and resultRegion() returns an error rather than choosing an occurrence. The epilogue is now structurally outside the region whatever it prints. Two cases pin it: a workspace whose NAME carries the marker produces no region at all, and a chatty epilogue does not become rows of the statement it follows.

Still true, still by convention: a statement containing two statements has both outputs folded into one region, and a statement returning no result set parses to [] indistinguishably from a header with no rows. identity-isolation.test.mjs asserts statically that every mutation case carries RETURNING, which is what makes the second safe. Both are recorded in the driver's own comment.

D9 (LOW) — REPAIRED, as a corrected claim rather than as a changed mechanism. WAS: rls-assertions.mjs argued that matching on message text is legitimate because "LC_ALL=C is set by the driver and by CI, so the English text is the text". The premise is true and the inference is not: `permission denied for table ...` and `new row violates row-level security policy for table ...` are SERVER-generated, so their language is the server's lc_messages GUC, which the client's environment does not reach and which is SUSET, so the driver cannot set it through PGOPTIONS either. LC_ALL=C governs libpq's own client-side text, a different set of messages.

IS NOW: the comment says that, and says why it was a wrong guarantee rather than an unsafe one -- against a server with a localised lc_messages, denialLayer returns null and expectDeniedBy THROWS naming the message it could not attribute, while expectDenied is unaffected because SQLSTATE is locale-independent. A new case drives a localised refusal through both and pins that the refusal still classifies, the layer does not, and a case declaring EITHER layer fails rather than passing on the catch-all arm. In CI the postgres:17 image initdbs under en_US.utf8, which is why the English text arrives there.

BATCH 021's OWN OPEN ITEMS, recorded by A1 Identity/Business rather than left for a reviewer to find. 021 lands app.workspace_member_scopes with its two policies and grants, five SECURITY INVOKER scope helpers, four RESTRICTIVE narrowing policies on batch 020's tables, and six permissive policies implementing §8.1's editor `P`. Five things it decides or declines, each of which a reviewer should disagree with here rather than discover in a predicate.

WHAT AN ABSENT SCOPE ROW MEANS IS A DECISION NO DOCUMENT MAKES. §7 fixes three scope types and says nothing about a member who holds none. 021 reads absence as NOT NARROWED: 010's own table comment already models scope as narrowing a ceiling and never widening it, and the fixture catalog describes user_owner_a and user_viewer_a with no scope at all, so the other reading would make `owner-a-sees-business-a1` false and would silently revoke Business access from every member nobody has scoped. The asymmetry that follows is the design and is asserted by cases in both directions: a `Y` operation is narrowed by scope where scope exists (member_scope_admits_*, true for an unscoped member) and a `P` operation requires an EXPLICIT scope (member_scope_covers_*, false for one). If the Product Owner wants absence to deny, that is an RFC and a data migration, not a predicate change.

A MEMBER SCOPE CAN BE CREATED AND NOT REMOVED THROUGH THE REQUEST PATH. §8.1's "Invite/change scope" is Y for owner and 021 writes the CREATE half. There is no UPDATE and no DELETE, for any role, because §8.5 forbids a broad user delete and requires a soft delete "ที่ update typed lifecycle field" and NO DOCUMENT NAMES A LIFECYCLE FIELD FOR THIS ROW. 010 could lean on §10 and §11.4 for an invitation's revoked_at; there is no equivalent sentence here, so the field is not invented. The refusal is at the PRIVILEGE layer and two cases assert it. Owed to whichever batch defines the lifecycle.

NO ROSTER READ ON THE SCOPE TABLE, so an owner may create a scope row for another member and may not read one back. §8.1's "Member list SELECT" is Y for owner and admin, and 011 implemented exactly that shape on app.workspace_members. It is not repeated here because the scope helpers resolve the caller from THIS table's own policy rather than by calling auth.uid() -- a `language sql` body is re-parsed in the calling session and would need USAGE on schema auth, which the CI shim grants to nobody and which no migration of ours can grant on the platform (011's header, measured) -- so a roster policy would widen what every helper sees. The two cannot both be had in this batch; the narrower one is taken. It also means an INSERT for another member cannot carry RETURNING, because Postgres applies SELECT policies to a returning clause.

THE POLICY THE BATCH RESTS ON IS PINNED AGAINST THE MIGRATION TEXT AND NOT AGAINST A DEPARSED CATALOG STRING. RFC-2026-020 §6.1/5 pins app_authz's policy by `pg_get_expr`, and that literal was DERIVED FROM A MEASUREMENT -- PostgreSQL 17.6's own deparser, read read-only off the provisioned instance. Nobody has deparsed 021's policy on any database, and writing a plausible-looking deparse would be inventing a measurement. The text pin holds today and the catalog pin is owed to whoever first applies 021 somewhere a `pg_get_expr` can be read off.

THE DEFERRED FK §6's REGISTRY NAMES IN THIS BATCH IS NOT CREATED, and that is a decision rather than an omission. 020 already recorded that `version_number`, unique per parent, answers "which version is latest" without a `current_version_id` pointer. Three more reasons are in 021's header and pinned by a test: a pointer is a second source of truth for "latest"; nothing in this schema could keep it true, because no command function binds the current row and its version into one transaction, and a DEFERRABLE constraint is checked only at COMMIT so RLS cannot enforce it; and it would need an UPDATE grant on a column no client should choose the value of, on the two tables §8.1 guards most carefully. §5 names no such column. If a later batch introduces that command function the pointer becomes checkable and that batch can propose it.

WORKSPACE LIFECYCLE VISIBILITY IS STILL NOT ENFORCED on the business and page tables. 021 narrows that surface and does not touch the gap; it is unchanged from batch 020's entry below and is owed to an RFC plus batch 170.
Gate G0 remains Specification Baseline Complete / External Verification Pending.

RFC-2026-012 (approved 2026-09-02) AND §9.1 COLLIDE OVER THE INDUSTRY CATALOG, AND BATCH 030 RESOLVED IT BY REFUSING A CELL RATHER THAN BY QUOTING ONE DOCUMENT AT THE OTHER. §9.1 classifies `PUBLIC-0` -- "published industry catalog, public model label" -- with "Client projection: allowed". RFC-2026-012 §2 says direct client reads go through named `security_invoker` views and never a base table, "including where a base table would be safe today", and §3 says the read allowlist starts empty and each entry is added BY RFC, not by a pull request. The allowlist is still empty: `exposed_views` in db/foundation/lint/catalog-snapshot.json measures [].

THE TWO DO NOT CONTRADICT, and the RFC's own "crux" section is why: it is about which TIER issues a statement, and its finding is that a policy "constrains the content of the row and the identity of the session; it says nothing about the tier, and RLS has no predicate that could". §9.1 is a statement of the same kind one level up -- it classifies CONTENT and licenses a projection, naming no object, no tier and no mechanism. RFC-2026-012 names all three and sits at position 1 of CONTRIBUTING_AGENTS.md's conflict order where the data package sits at 4. So §9.1 licenses the content and RFC-2026-012 licenses the object, and batch 030 can satisfy only the first.

WHAT 030 DID: created app.industry_packs and app.industry_pack_versions with ENABLE and FORCE row level security, NO policy, and NO grant to `authenticated` or `anon`. The published catalog exists, is immutable, and is unreachable from the request path. Four isolation cases assert that as a GRANT-layer refusal from both tenants and from anonymous, which is what an empty allowlist looks like from the outside, and a static test scans EVERY migration for a grant or a view that would open it.

WHAT IS OWED, AND TO WHOM. (1) An RFC that adds the first allowlist entry. It is LARGER THAN IT LOOKS: §8.5 requires an exposed view to be `security_invoker = true`, and such a view is evaluated with the CALLER's privileges on the base table -- so the entry is a view AND a column-scoped SELECT grant to `authenticated` AND a SELECT policy admitting it, three objects in one decision. Owner: A0 Architecture/Integration with A1 Security, per RFC-2026-012 itself. (2) Whether `anon` may read a PUBLIC-0 catalog at all. A published catalog is the one family in this schema an anonymous reader could plausibly be given; §8.5 says anonymous holds no TENANT policy and says nothing about a global one. Granting it decides that the product has an unauthenticated surface, which is A1 Security's through an RFC and not a batch's. (3) The policy that lets the Core Runtime read a pack. §8's four matrices contain NO ROW for an industry pack anywhere, so there is no cell to implement and 010's rule holds -- "a grant issued ahead of the thing that needs it is a grant nobody reviews against a caller". Owed to the batch that brings the resolver, 070 at the earliest by §6's registry.

WHAT BATCH 030 INHERITED AND DID NOT WIDEN. Batches 010, 020 and 021 grant `authenticated` SELECT on base tables, which RFC-2026-012 §2 also names. That gap is real and is not fixed here: migration invariant 1 forbids rewriting a merged migration, and A1's condition 2 on the RFC puts the lint that would catch it -- "no exposed table grants INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to `authenticated`" -- in DB-00 as an RLS change needing its own RFC. It has not landed. What makes 030 not a repetition of that gap is that every one of those grants is bounded by a predicate RLS can express, `app.is_active_member(workspace_id)`, so a leak reaches one workspace and the isolation suite proves the boundary. A GLOBAL catalog has no such predicate: the only thing between an authenticated caller and the whole table would be the column grant, which is exactly the failure §2 names -- "column drift is silent, and RLS filters rows, not columns". §2's reason is prospective on a tenant table and load-bearing here.

TWO FINDINGS IN THE BASELINE THAT BATCH 030 RECORDED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT, both owned by A1 Data and neither an agent's to close (§15).

(1) §5 assigns industry.core the retention classes `CATALOG/HISTORY`, and **§10 DEFINES NO `CATALOG` CLASS**. Its table has twenty-six rows and none of them is that one. `HISTORY` is defined as "อายุ Workspace + lineage", which cannot describe a global catalog row that outlives every workspace. Batch 030 encodes no retention window: batch 160 owns the retention job and §10's own Product/Security/Legal approval owns the number. A migration that had written a number into a constraint would have made an undefined class read as ratified.

(2) §8's four RLS matrices contain NO ROW for an industry pack, anywhere. RFC-2026-012's own inventory says as much -- it classifies the family from §9 and labels the row an INFERENCE the author agrees with rather than a statement of the baseline. So the global tables have no cell to implement and every operation on them is denied by default, which is what batch 030 shipped. The TENANT table is different and the inference is stated rather than hidden: §8.1's two Business rows govern app.industry_assignments, because 020's own header named the industry pack assignment as part of a Business's attribute surface while deferring it to this batch. If A1 Data disagrees with that reading, the policies to change are the six in 030_industry.sql and the cases that assert them, not a silence anyone has to notice.
